name: Early-ripening Champa rice in Song China
summary: In 1012 the Song court sent drought-resistant, early-ripening Champa rice seed from Fujian to drought-struck farmers, and the variety then drew wide attention across China's rice lands.
description: After a severe drought in the Yangtze and Huai valleys in 1012, Emperor Zhenzong had envoys procure 30,000 bushels of Champa rice seed in Fujian and distribute it to farmers in the drought areas with instructions on how to grow it. The rice, which had come from the Champa kingdom in what is now central Vietnam at an unknown earlier date, ripened early, resisted drought and was not sensitive to day length; farmers later selected higher-yielding forms of it. Ho Ping-ti held that this began the spread of early-ripening rice in China, which other historians question.

impact.note: Early-ripening rice spread through the rice lands of southern China over generations (reach 2), as a better variety of a crop already grown, whose share in later double cropping and population growth historians dispute (depth 1), with farmers' later selections as its successors (generativity 1).

why: A severe drought in the Yangtze and Huai river valleys in 1012 led the emperor to turn to a rice known to resist drought and ripen early.

date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Some put the arrival of Champa rice as early as the eighth century; from 1012 onward it began to receive widespread attention in China.

evidence.supports: Some say it was as early as the eighth century, but from 1012 onward, Champa rice began to receive widespread attention in China

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The article draws on Ho (1956) for the 1012 distribution; the Song text of the edict was not seen.
The source gives Zhenzong's reign as 992 to 1022, which does not match the usual 997 to 1022; only the 1012 date is used.
When Champa rice first reached Fujian is unknown; the source reports a claim of the eighth century.
How much of the Song rise in double cropping, output and population is owed to Champa rice is disputed (Ho against Perkins and Zeng).

research.note: The source says the rice came to China from the Champa Kingdom in what is now central Vietnam, reaching Fujian first.
